items.text: ++ and -- are the increment and decrement operators: shorthand that adds 1 to (or subtracts 1 from) a numeric variable.
++ has the same effect as i = i + 1 and -- the same as i = i - 1; as statements i++ and ++i are the same, but in expressions ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

i++: fetch the value of i (that is the expression's value), then store i + 1 into i. ++i: store i + 1 into i, and the new value is the expression's value. Both happen before the rest of the enclosing expression continues.
With i = 5: x = i++ gives x = 5, i = 6; x = ++i gives x = 6, i = 6; i = i++ leaves i = 5.
One execution changes exactly one variable (i) by exactly 1 and returns its old (i++) or new (++i) value.
The usual for-loop update is i++ (shorthand for i = i + 1); as a stand-alone update statement ++i and i++ give the same loop.
Inside a larger expression the result depends on which value (old or new) the increment yields and on left-to-right evaluation, e.g. j += j++ in Exercise 1.3.6.
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1 (and i += k for i = i + k), so it changes the variable's stored value.
i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
Plan/role: the update of a stepper or counter (count++ in a counter, i++ in a counted loop).
As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.
Use i++ / i-- as stand-alone statements and in for-loop updates; avoid them inside larger expressions (x = ++i), as the book does, and use += for steps other than 1.

answer: They are all for-each loops.

items.text: In for (int x : a), x takes the index values 0, 1, ..., a.length - 1.
In for (int x : a), x takes the element values a[0], a[1] and so on.
Assigning x = v inside for (int x : a) changes the array element.
x is a copy of the element, so assigning to x does not change the array.
Identity: the enhanced for loop ('for each' loop), a statement that runs its body once per element of an array, giving the body each element value.
Declarative: 'for (T x : a) statement', where T is the element type (or a type it converts to); x's scope is the contained statement.

Sequencing: equivalent to for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { T x = a[i]; body }. The element is copied into x, the body runs, and then the next element follows, until all a.length elements are done.
Result: the body runs a.length times with x = a[0], a[1], ...; for int[] a = {1, 2, 3}, summing x gives 6. The loop itself produces no value.
State transition: each pass sets x to the next element value; assigning to x changes only x, never a[i].
It is a full forward traversal with the index hidden, so it cannot skip, go backward, stop at a computed index or write a[i].
Plan/role: accumulate or count over all values (gatherer or counter role) when the position is irrelevant, as in histogram counting counts[score]++.
Conservation: rewriting an index loop as a for-each keeps every read of a[i] but breaks writes to the array (assigning x has no effect) and loses i, so searches can no longer report positions.

Applicability: use for-each to read every element in order when the index is not needed (sums, counts, printing). Use an index loop when you need the position, write elements, visit part of the array, go backward, or compare neighbours.

Arithmetic operators: the binary operators + - * / % that combine two numeric operands into a numeric result.

Both operands must be numeric, and the result has the promoted type (int, long or double). * / % bind tighter than + -, all group left to right, and int / or % by zero throws ArithmeticException. Unary minus negates its operand (-x) and unary plus leaves it unchanged; they bind more tightly than * and /, so -a * b is (-a) * b.
The left operand is evaluated fully, then the right operand, and then the operator is applied in the promoted type.
With ints, 17 / 3 is 5 and 17 % 3 is 2. With doubles, 5.0 / 3.0 is 1.6666666666666667. With mixed operands, the int is promoted first (10 / 3.0 is 3.333...).
An arithmetic operator never changes its operands. Each variable is replaced by its value, and only an assignment (or ++ or op=) stores the result.
Operators build larger expressions from smaller ones, and each operand can itself be any expression.
For ints, / gives the truncated quotient and % the remainder, so (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
int / or % by zero throws a run-time exception, while floating-point division by zero gives Infinity or NaN.

+ adds when both operands are numbers and concatenates when either operand is a String, converting the other operand to a String. It is left-associative, so 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" but "1" + 2 + 3 is "123".
Arithmetic operators turn formulas into code: totals, averages, unit conversions (inch * CM_PER_INCH), and digit extraction (n % 10, n / 10).

Changing an operand's type changes the operator's meaning (int / versus double /). Reordering * and / changes integer results (59 * 100 / 60 is 98, 59 / 60 * 100 is 0). Replacing ^ with Math.pow gives a real power.
Use the operators for arithmetic on numeric types. Use the Math library for powers, roots and absolute values, and parse numeric Strings before computing with them.

items.text: Integer division: / applied to two integer operands, giving the whole-number quotient with the fractional part discarded.
If both operands of / are integral types, the result is an integer that rounds toward 0 (-14 / 3 is -4). If either operand is a double, the division is floating point.

Each / is evaluated when its turn comes (precedence, then left to right), using the types of its own two operands. Promoting the result to double, by a cast or by assignment, happens only afterwards and cannot restore the lost fraction.
q = a / b stores the truncated quotient in q and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, an ArithmeticException stops execution before anything is stored.
/ and % on ints are paired: q = a / b and r = a % b always satisfy a = b * q + r.
Normalizing counts must divide as doubles. With two ints, counts / total truncates to 0 whenever counts < total.
% gives the remainder of the same truncating division: (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
Quotient plans: unit conversion (76 / 12 feet), dropping a digit (n / 10), finding a midpoint ((lo + hi) / 2), and computing a bucket or row index (i / cols).

Making one operand a double (10.0 / 3) keeps the fraction (3.333...). Casting after the division does not. Multiplying before dividing preserves precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98). Changing an operand's sign changes only the quotient's sign, since rounding is toward zero.

Use integer division when you want the whole quotient (units, digits, indices, half a size). When a fraction is needed, make one operand a double (10.0 / 3 or (double) a / b) rather than turning every variable into a double.

The if-else statement is a two-way conditional: it executes one of two statements (or blocks) depending on a boolean condition.
Syntax: if (<boolean expression>) <statements T> else <statements F>; it executes one or the other, but not both: T if the condition is true, F otherwise.
Evaluate the condition once; if true execute the then branch, otherwise execute the else branch; then continue with the statement after the whole if-else (the condition is not re-tested).
Exactly one branch's effects occur; e.g. if (x > y) max = x; else max = y; leaves max equal to the larger value, and the coin flip prints either Heads or Tails, never both.
One execution reads the condition's variables and applies the effects of exactly one branch; a change made by the then branch to the condition's variables cannot cause the else branch to run.
if-else is an if with a second branch for the false case; dropping the else gives a plain if in which the false case does nothing.
Either branch may itself be an if or if-else, which nests conditionals; without braces an inner else pairs with the innermost if.
c ? a : b is the expression form of if (c) v = a; else v = b;: it yields a value of one branch, evaluating only the selected operand.
An else-if chain is an if-else whose else part is another if-else, repeated; the final else catches all remaining cases.
Plan: two-way choice / alternative action - compute one of two results (max of two values, heads or tails, error message or quotient).

Swapping the two branches and negating the condition preserves behaviour; swapping the branches alone inverts it. Replacing if-else with two separate ifs is not equivalent when the then branch changes a variable used in the condition.

Use if-else when exactly one of two actions must happen; use a plain if when nothing happens in the false case, an else-if chain or switch for more than two mutually exclusive cases, and c ? a : b when you only need to choose a value.

Running (executing) a program is launching it with java Name so that the Java Virtual Machine follows its instructions.

++ and -- are the increment and decrement operators: shorthand that adds 1 to (or subtracts 1 from) a numeric variable.
++ has the same effect as i = i + 1 and -- the same as i = i - 1; as statements i++ and ++i are the same, but in expressions ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

i++: fetch the value of i (that is the expression's value), then store i + 1 into i. ++i: store i + 1 into i, and the new value is the expression's value. Both happen before the rest of the enclosing expression continues.
With i = 5: x = i++ gives x = 5, i = 6; x = ++i gives x = 6, i = 6; i = i++ leaves i = 5.
One execution changes exactly one variable (i) by exactly 1 and returns its old (i++) or new (++i) value.
The usual for-loop update is i++ (shorthand for i = i + 1); as a stand-alone update statement ++i and i++ give the same loop.
Inside a larger expression the result depends on which value (old or new) the increment yields and on left-to-right evaluation, e.g. j += j++ in Exercise 1.3.6.
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1 (and i += k for i = i + k), so it changes the variable's stored value.
i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
Plan/role: the update of a stepper or counter (count++ in a counter, i++ in a counted loop).
As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.
Use i++ / i-- as stand-alone statements and in for-loop updates; avoid them inside larger expressions (x = ++i), as the book does, and use += for steps other than 1.
